title: Strong and Stable Structures
seo_title: Grade 3 Science: Strong and Stable Structures Worksheets (Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Describe structures as natural or human-made; explain how shape, materials and a wide base make structures strong and stable; design, build and test structures that hold a load. (summary of the Ontario Science and Technology curriculum, 2022, Strand D: Structures and Mechanisms – Strong and Stable Structures)
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 science worksheets on natural and human-made structures, strong shapes, stability, materials and testing structures. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Strong structures hold loads; stable ones do not tip.
key_sub: Triangles, arches and wide bases make structures strong and stable.
body_html:
How to think about it

A structure is something built to support or hold a load.

  • Natural structures: nests, webs, beaver dams. Human-made: houses, bridges, the CN Tower.
  • Strong shapes include triangles, arches, domes and tubes.
  • Stable structures have a wide base and keep heavy parts low.
Example

How can you make a block tower more stable?

wider base

heavy blocks at the bottom

Answer: make the base wider

Example

Why is a triangle strong?

it does not squish

Answer: it keeps its shape

Common mistakes

  • Thinking taller structures are always better.
  • Thinking only heavy materials make strong structures.
  • Thinking shape does not matter.

faq.q: What is the difference between strong and stable?
faq.a: A strong structure holds a load without breaking. A stable structure does not tip over.

faq.q: Why are triangles used in bridges?
faq.a: A triangle cannot change shape unless a side breaks, so it is very strong.
They add loads and push on them to see if they bend, break or tip, then improve the design.

items.q: Why are bricks good for building walls?
c: They are hard, strong when stacked and do not burn.
items.e: Bricks resist squeezing.

items.q: What does a building's foundation do?
c: spreads the weight into the ground so it does not sink
items.e: Foundations are under the ground.

items.q: Ava says B was built from all the blocks in A. Is that true?
c: Yes. They are both made of blocks.
No. A has 7 blocks and B has 5.
Yes. B is a new shape, so it must be the same.
items.e: Count the blocks in each building.

items.q: What makes a structure stable?
c: a wide base and a low centre of weight
items.e: Stable structures do not tip over.

items.q: Owen wants to make a cooking pot. Which material is best?
items.e: Metal is best because it is strong and does not burn or melt on the stove.

items.q: Which material is best for building a strong bridge for a toy car?
c: wooden craft sticks glued into triangles
items.e: Shape and material both matter.

items.q: Benjamin makes a fence post out of wood. Why is wood a good choice?
c: Because it is smooth and shiny so it reflects.
Because it is the prettiest colour.
Because it is hard and strong.
Because it is light and blocks the sun.
items.e: Choose a material by its properties, not its colour.

items.q: Why are glass windows thick in tall buildings?
c: Thicker glass is stronger against wind.
items.e: Thickness adds strength.

items.q: Maya took apart building A and built B. Could Maya have used all the same blocks?
c: No. B looks bigger, so it has more blocks.
No. A looks taller, so it has more blocks.
No. Blocks disappear when you take them apart.
items.e: Count both: 9 and 9. Same pieces, new shape.

items.q: Why are snow forts built with thick walls at the bottom?
c: Thick bottoms hold the weight of the snow above.
To make the fort taller only.
Snow is lighter at the bottom.
items.e: Bottoms carry the load.

items.q: Why do igloos keep their shape?
c: The dome shape spreads the weight evenly.
items.e: Domes are strong shapes.

items.q: Which structure uses an arch?
c: a stone bridge over a creek
items.e: Arches carry weight to the ground.

items.q: Which material bends without breaking, making it good for a fishing rod?
items.e: Flexible materials can bend.

items.q: Why do bridges over wide rivers often have many pillars?
c: Each pillar holds up part of the weight, so the bridge does not sag.
items.e: Supports share the load.

items.q: Which material would make the best roof for a doghouse?
items.e: Roofs must keep water out.

items.q: A tower of blocks falls over. How could you make it more stable?
c: use fewer blocks at the bottom
put the heaviest blocks on top
items.e: A wide base improves stability.

items.q: Ava says B was built from all the blocks in A. Is that true?
c: No. A has 12 blocks and B has 10.
Yes. They are both made of blocks.
Yes. B is a new shape, so it must be the same.
items.e: Count the blocks in each building.

items.q: Emma says B was built from all the blocks in A. Is that true?
c: No. A has 6 blocks and B has 8.
Yes. They are both made of blocks.
Yes. B is a new shape, so it must be the same.
items.e: Count the blocks in each building.

items.q: Ava makes a sun hat out of straw. Why is straw a good choice?
c: Because it is the prettiest colour.
Because it keeps water out and bends.
Because it is light and blocks the sun.
items.e: Choose a material by its properties, not its colour.

items.q: Maya makes a lunch bag you can use again out of cloth. Why is cloth a good choice?
c: Because it is strong and bends.
Because it is the prettiest colour.
Because it bends and keeps water in.
items.e: Choose a material by its properties, not its colour.

items.q: Aiden built a house with 11 blocks. He took it apart and used all the blocks to build a train. How many blocks are in the train?
items.e: Same pieces, so still 11 blocks.

items.q: Why is a triangle a strong shape for building?
c: It keeps its shape when pushed.
items.e: Squares can squish into a diamond shape.

items.q: Mateo takes apart a bike. What will Mateo find?
c: smaller pieces: wheels, a frame, pedals and a seat
items.e: Big objects are made of smaller pieces.

items.q: Liam takes apart a block castle. What will Liam find?
items.e: Big objects are made of smaller pieces.

items.q: Why should playground equipment be tested?
c: to make sure it is strong, stable and safe for children
items.e: Safety comes first.

items.q: Sofia takes apart a toy car. What will Sofia find?
c: smaller pieces: wheels, a body and a seat
items.e: Big objects are made of smaller pieces.

items.q: Benjamin built a boat with 18 blocks. He took it apart and used all the blocks to build a wall. How many blocks are in the wall?
items.e: Same pieces, so still 18 blocks.

items.q: Owen's block wall weighs 110 grams. He takes it apart and builds a boat with all the same blocks. How much does the boat weigh?
items.e: Same pieces, so the weight stays the same.

items.q: Why do tents need stakes and ropes?
c: to make them heavier to carry
to keep them stable in the wind
items.e: Ropes and stakes hold the tent down.

items.q: Hana takes apart a necklace. What will Hana find?
c: smaller pieces: beads and a string
items.e: Big objects are made of smaller pieces.

items.q: What is a load?
c: the weight or force a structure holds
items.e: A shelf holds a load of books.

items.q: Mei's block train weighs 180 grams. She takes it apart and builds a house with all the same blocks. How much does the house weigh?
items.e: Same pieces, so the weight stays the same.

items.q: Which is a natural structure?
items.e: Natural structures are not made by people.

items.q: Ethan takes apart a sandwich. What will Ethan find?
c: smaller pieces: bread, cheese and lettuce
items.e: Big objects are made of smaller pieces.

items.q: Ethan's block boat weighs 250 grams. He takes it apart and builds a robot with all the same blocks. How much does the robot weigh?
items.e: Same pieces, so the weight stays the same.

items.q: Which joint lets a door swing open?
items.e: Hinges let parts move.

items.q: What is a structure?
c: something built to support or hold something
items.e: Houses, bridges, chairs and nests are structures.

items.q: Why is a cardboard box stronger with its flaps taped down?
c: The closed shape holds together and spreads the load.
items.e: Closed shapes are stronger.

items.q: Maya takes apart a puzzle. What will Maya find?
items.e: Big objects are made of smaller pieces.

items.q: Priya takes apart a paper chain. What will Priya find?
items.e: Big objects are made of smaller pieces.

items.q: Which is the strongest way to join two craft sticks?
c: glue them and let the glue dry fully
items.e: Strong joints make strong structures.

items.q: A cup on a table is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: The forces on it are unbalanced.
Gravity pulls it down and the table pushes it up with an equal force.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: The cart is at rest. What will happen?
c: It will move to the left.
It will move to the right.
items.e: Balanced forces do not change the motion of an object at rest.

items.q: A plant pot on a windowsill is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: The forces on it are unbalanced.
Gravity pulls it down and the windowsill pushes it up with an equal force.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: How can you make a sheet of paper strong enough to hold a book?
c: fold it into a zigzag or roll it into a tube
items.e: Shape adds strength.

items.q: Why are most houses in Ontario built with wood frames?
c: Wood is strong, light, easy to cut and grows in Canada.
items.e: Materials are chosen for their properties.

items.q: Two forces act on a desk. The arrows are the same length. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced?
items.e: Equal forces in opposite directions are balanced.

items.q: A ball on the floor is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: Gravity pulls it down and the floor pushes it up with an equal force.
The forces on it are unbalanced.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: A chair wobbles. What is the most likely problem?
c: one leg is shorter or loose
the chair is the wrong colour
items.e: All legs must touch the floor evenly.

items.q: What makes a structure strong?
c: it can hold a load without breaking or bending too much
items.e: Strength is about holding loads.

items.q: A box on a bench is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: The forces on it are unbalanced.
Gravity pulls it down and the bench pushes it up with an equal force.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: A toy on a bed is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: Gravity pulls it down and the bed pushes it up with an equal force.
The forces on it are unbalanced.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: Why might a builder choose recycled materials?
c: to reduce waste and save resources
items.e: Recycling helps the environment.

items.q: A rock on the ground is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: Gravity pulls it down and the ground pushes it up with an equal force.
The forces on it are unbalanced.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: Two forces act on a toy car that is at rest. One arrow is longer. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced?
items.e: The forces are not equal, so they are unbalanced.

items.q: A laptop on a desk is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: Gravity pulls it down and the desk pushes it up with an equal force.
The forces on it are unbalanced.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: Why are the heaviest blocks placed at the bottom of a tower?
c: It keeps the weight low so the tower is stable.
items.e: Heavy parts belong at the bottom.

items.q: The box is at rest. What will happen?
c: It will move to the left.
It will move to the right.
items.e: Balanced forces do not change the motion of an object at rest.

items.q: A book on a shelf is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: Gravity pulls it down and the shelf pushes it up with an equal force.
The forces on it are unbalanced.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: The cart is at rest. The arrows show two forces. What will happen?
c: It will start to move to the right.
It will move up into the air.
It will start to move to the left.
items.e: The bigger force points to the left, so the forces are unbalanced and the cart moves that way.

items.q: Noah makes a bouncy ball out of rubber. Why is rubber a good choice?
c: Because it is the prettiest colour.
Because it is strong and does not burn or melt on the stove.
Because it is hard and strong.
items.e: Choose a material by its properties, not its colour.

items.q: What can you make with the blocks from a tower?
c: a bigger tower with more blocks
a new object, like a bridge or a car
items.e: Same pieces, new shape.

items.q: Why do spider webs hold insects without breaking?
c: Spider silk is made of steel.
The web is glued to the Moon.
The silk is strong and stretchy and the web spreads the force.
items.e: Webs are natural structures.

items.q: Chloe wants to make a fence post. Which material is best?
items.e: Wood is best because it is hard and strong.

items.q: Which is a human-made structure?
items.e: People design and build human-made structures.

items.q: Sofia built a bridge. How many blocks did Sofia use?
items.e: Count every block: 7.

items.q: Liam makes a boat out of wood. Why is wood a good choice?
c: Because it is the prettiest colour.
Because it is light and blocks the sun.
Because it bends and keeps water in.
items.e: Choose a material by its properties, not its colour.

items.q: Ethan hangs a weight from a spring. The spring stretches, then stops. Why does the weight stop moving?
c: The spring pulls up with the same force as gravity pulls down.
items.e: The forces become balanced.

items.q: Emma's shirt test: cotton dried in 30 minutes, wool in 90. Which dried faster?
c: they dried at the same time
items.e: Fewer minutes means faster.

c: Friction pushes back with the same force, so the forces are balanced.
items.e: Balanced forces do not change motion.

items.q: Why are hydro towers built with many triangles?
c: Triangles make the frame strong and rigid.
items.e: Frames use triangles for strength.

items.q: Hana tested which material holds the most water drops before leaking. Which material should Hana use for a cup?
items.e: The tallest bar held the most drops: plastic.

items.q: In a tug-of-war, the Red Team has 4 kids and the Gold Team has 6 kids. Every kid pulls equally hard. What happens to the rope?
c: It moves toward the Red Team.
It moves toward the Gold Team.
items.e: The Gold Team pulls with more force, so the forces are unbalanced.

items.q: Ava weighs a block tower: 150 grams. She builds a bridge from the same blocks. What will the bridge weigh?
items.e: Same pieces, same weight.

items.q: Olivia tested which material holds the most water drops before leaking. Which material should Olivia use for a cup?
items.e: The tallest bar held the most drops: foil.

items.q: In a tug-of-war, the Green Team has 5 kids and the Gold Team has 6 kids. Every kid pulls equally hard. What happens to the rope?
c: It moves toward the Gold Team.
It moves toward the Green Team.
items.e: The Gold Team pulls with more force, so the forces are unbalanced.

items.q: Ava's paper bridge held 4 pennies. Her cardboard bridge held 20. Which is stronger?
items.e: 20 is more than 4.

items.q: Kai tested how many water drops each material held before leaking. Which material leaked first?
items.e: The shortest bar held the fewest drops: felt.

items.q: Ava pushes a toy car gently and then hard. Which push makes it move farther?
items.e: A bigger force changes motion more.

items.q: Leah tested how many water drops each material held before leaking. Which material leaked first?
items.e: The shortest bar held the fewest drops: cloth.

items.q: A sled is sliding down a snowy hill. A friend pulls it from the bottom with a rope. What happens?
items.e: The pull is opposite to the motion, so it slows the sled.

items.q: In a tug-of-war, the Green Team has 6 kids and the Gold Team has 6 kids. Every kid pulls equally hard. What happens to the rope?
c: It moves toward the Green Team.
It moves toward the Gold Team.
It breaks because there are no forces.
It does not move, because the pulls are balanced.
items.e: Equal pulls in opposite directions are balanced forces.

items.q: Olivia wants to test how the size of a push changes how far a ball rolls. What should she change?
c: only the size of the push
items.e: Change one variable for a fair test.

items.q: An engineer builds a bridge from 30 beams. She takes it apart to build a tower. What should she check first?
c: the weight of the tower she has not built
items.e: Count the pieces.

items.q: Mateo has 20 blocks. He builds a house with 14. How many are left for a dog house?
Why should Kai test each material the same way?
items.e: A fair test compares fairly.

items.q: A roof test: plastic leaked 0 drops, cloth leaked 9. Which is best for a roof?
items.e: 0 drops leaked.
